description: Team Incredibles is pioneering the Earth Information Jukebox, a dynamic platform designed to aggregate, harmonize, and stream global planetary data on demand. By converting complex satellite telemetry, climate metrics, and ecological feeds into accessible, high-density digital streams, the initiative allows researchers, policymakers, and communities to select and visualize vital environmental insights.
summary:
EARTH//SOUND – NASA Earth Information Center Multi-Sensory Jukebox

EARTH//SOUND is an interactive, accessibility-minded platform that transforms NASA Earth-observation visualizations into immersive soundscapes. Using imagery and animations from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio, we developed a system that translates visual patterns—such as brightness, colour, spatial contrast, and changes across frames—into pitch, rhythm, timbre, and stereo audio.

The platform combines an interactive browser-based synthesizer, multiple musical scales, narration, image and video uploads, before-and-after comparisons, image-based diagnostics, and downloadable stereo WAV soundscapes. It also offers optional AI-generated explanations to make complex visualizations easier to understand.

By turning environmental imagery into something people can both see and hear, EARTH//SOUND addresses the challenge of making planetary information more engaging, intuitive, and accessible. It offers researchers, students, policymakers, and the wider public an alternative way to explore Earth’s interconnected systems. We believe that when people can experience environmental information through multiple senses, complex scientific ideas become more approachable—and awareness of our planet becomes more meaningful.
details:
Project Details – EARTH//SOUND

NASA Earth Information Center Multi-Sensory Jukebox | Team SUPERNOVA FAMILY

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

EARTH//SOUND is an interactive platform that transforms Earth-observation visualizations into soundscapes, allowing users to experience environmental information through both sight and hearing.

The project uses imagery, previews, and animations from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS). Users can explore a curated collection of visualizations covering ocean currents, sea surface temperatures, atmospheric carbon dioxide, forest height, air quality, aerosols, lightning, night lights, and the water cycle.

The application processes the visual characteristics of selected images or sampled video frames, including brightness, colour, saturation, edges, and spatial contrast. It divides the imagery into horizontal bands and columns, then maps extracted visual patterns to musical characteristics such as pitch, harmony, timbre, rhythm, timing, and stereo positioning.

Users can interact with the resulting soundscape through a browser-based synthesizer, select different musical scales, explore individual image regions, and listen to spoken narration. They can also upload their own images or videos, compare two images to explore visual differences, and generate downloadable stereo WAV audio files using the Python audio engine.

An optional AI-powered analyst can provide plain-language explanations of visual patterns, helping users engage with complex environmental imagery.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • Multisensory learning: Converts visual environmental information into sound, offering an alternative way to explore complex planetary systems.
  • Accessibility: Includes keyboard interaction, screen-reader announcements, spoken narration, and audio-based exploration to support users with different accessibility needs.
  • Greater engagement: Makes satellite visualizations more interactive and encourages users to explore environmental information rather than simply viewing static images.
  • Educational value: Helps students and the public engage with topics such as ocean circulation, atmospheric conditions, biodiversity, and human impacts on Earth.
  • Flexible exploration: Supports NASA visualization collections as well as user-uploaded images, videos, and before-and-after comparisons.
  • Creative communication: Provides an alternative medium for communicating patterns in environmental imagery through music and sound.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make Earth-observation information more approachable, engaging, and inclusive. Environmental datasets and satellite visualizations contain valuable information, but they can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. EARTH//SOUND explores how sonification can create another entry point into this information.

We hope to encourage curiosity about Earth's interconnected systems, support multisensory science education, and inspire new ways of communicating environmental information. By allowing people to listen to visual patterns, the project demonstrates how technology and creativity can work together to make planetary science more accessible.

In the long term, we envision this concept developing into an educational and public-engagement tool for classrooms, science exhibitions, environmental awareness campaigns, and interactive digital experiences.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software did we use?

The project was developed primarily using Python, Streamlit, and browser-based web technologies.

Programming languages and technologies:

  • Python – Core application logic, image processing, feature extraction, and audio generation.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript – Interactive browser interface and synthesizer controls.
  • Web Audio API – Real-time browser-based sound synthesis and spatial audio.
  • Browser SpeechSynthesis API – Spoken narration and accessibility support.

Libraries and frameworks:

  • Streamlit – Interactive web application and user interface.
  • NumPy – Numerical processing and audio synthesis.
  • Pillow – Image loading, conversion, resizing, and processing.
  • Requests – Retrieval of NASA SVS API metadata and remote assets.
  • SciPy – Stereo WAV generation and audio export.
  • Matplotlib – Image diagnostics and visualizations.
  • ImageIO and imageio-ffmpeg – Video reading and frame sampling.

Data source and services:

  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) API and visualization assets.
  • Optional AI analysis through OpenRouter, Google Gemini, or OpenAI, depending on the user's configured API provider.

The project is software-based and does not require dedicated external hardware. It can be accessed through a web browser on a computer with an internet connection for live NASA visualization retrieval. Audio playback requires a compatible browser and audio output device.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The central creative idea behind EARTH//SOUND is to treat Earth imagery as a musical score.

Instead of limiting environmental visualizations to something users look at, we explore what happens when visual patterns become something they can hear. A brighter region, a change in spatial contrast, or a different distribution of colours can influence the resulting soundscape.

We also incorporated musical scales—including Lydian, Pentatonic, Dorian, and Harmonic Minor—to give users different ways of experiencing the same visual material. Latitude-band exploration, stereo positioning, transient accents, and atmospheric drone elements further contribute to the experience.

The combination of NASA visualizations, image processing, generative audio, narration, and optional AI commentary brings together scientific communication, accessibility, and creative technology in a single platform.

Importantly, EARTH//SOUND is an experimental sonification experience rather than a scientific measurement instrument. Its audio mappings are based on visual properties of rendered imagery and should not be interpreted as direct measurements of physical climate variables.

6. What factors did our team consider during development?

Our team considered several factors to ensure that the experience was useful, engaging, and responsible:

  • Scientific integrity: We distinguished visual image properties from actual physical measurements. Brightness and colour proxies are not presented as direct measurements of temperature, CO₂ concentration, ocean speed, or other environmental variables.
  • Accessibility and inclusion: We incorporated narration, keyboard controls, screen-reader announcements, and audio interaction to offer different ways of engaging with the platform.
  • Performance: NASA animations can be large, so we implemented frame sampling, resizing, and fallback options to make processing more manageable.
  • User experience: We designed interactive controls for selecting visualizations, adjusting sound settings, comparing images, and exporting audio.
  • Flexibility: We included support for both NASA-provided visualizations and user-uploaded images and videos.
  • Reliability: The application includes fallback behaviour for unavailable NASA assets and separates browser-based audio playback from Python-generated WAV rendering.
  • Responsible AI use: Optional AI-generated explanations are treated as supplementary commentary rather than verified scientific conclusions.
  • Educational relevance: We aimed to make the experience understandable to people without specialist knowledge of satellite data, environmental science, or audio engineering.

Ultimately, EARTH//SOUND reflects Team SUPERNOVA FAMILY's belief that scientific information does not have to be communicated through numbers and images alone. By bringing together planetary data, technology, sound, and accessibility, we want to give people a new way to connect with the planet we call home.
